intro: To clear site data for one website in Chrome on Mac, open Settings, go to Privacy and security, then Third-party cookies, and click See all site data and permissions. Search for the site, click the trash icon labeled Remove, and confirm Delete, which leaves every other site's data in place.
tldr: Open Settings, then Privacy and security, then Third-party cookies, then See all site data and permissions.
Search for the domain, click the trash icon labeled Remove, and confirm Delete.
Already on the site? Use the website settings icon left of the address bar, then Cookies and site data.
Clearing one site can sign you out of that site. It does not sign you out of other sites.
Command+Shift+Delete clears data for all sites, so skip it when only one site misbehaves.

blocks.text: Clearing one website's data is a narrow fix. You use it when one site loads wrong, keeps you signed in when you want out, or remembers a setting that no longer helps. Chrome lets you do this site by site, so the rest of your browsing stays put. This guide covers the Settings route, the address bar route, and the all-sites shortcut that you probably want to avoid for this job.
Before you start: three quick checks
Spend a minute on these checks before you delete anything. Each one prevents a common surprise.

items: Confirm the domain. Open the site and read the domain in the address bar, without https:// or any path after it.
Check that you can sign in. Know your password or have a way to reset it, because deleting site data can sign you out.
Decide between one site and all sites. One site is the right choice when only that site misbehaves.

blocks.text: What clearing one site's data removes

Site data is what a website leaves behind on your Mac. It includes cookies, which are small pieces of text that sites use to remember you. It also includes cached files, local storage, and IndexedDB, a database that a site keeps inside your browser.
Google's help pages list the same kinds of data, plus the site settings and permissions you have granted. Those include choices such as allowing notifications or camera access.

Clearing one site removes these items for that site only. Your other sites keep their sign-ins, cookies, and saved settings. That is the main reason to choose this route over the all-sites shortcut covered later.
What you will lose on that site

Google warns that deleting cookies may sign you out of sites that remember you. It can also delete saved site preferences. Expect to sign in again on the site you cleared, and expect any layout or language choices it remembered to reset.

Google's Android help page says deleting cookies while you are signed in to Chrome does not sign you out of your Google Account. That page is for Android, so treat it as a strong hint for the Mac, not a promise.
Remove one site's data in Chrome Settings

This is the route Google's desktop help page describes. The page does not use Mac-specific wording, so the names below are the ones it uses. Chrome ships a new update about every four weeks, so a label may shift. If one is missing, search Settings for the site name instead.
Type the domain, such as example.com, without https:// or the path. If you see two rows that look like the same site, delete both.
A worked example with a news site

Say a news site keeps loading an old layout. You open the site list and search for its domain. Three rows appear: the main domain, a subdomain used for images, and an ad network. You delete only the main domain and its image subdomain.

Reload the site in a new tab. The layout updates, and you stay signed in to your email and banking sites. The ad network keeps its data, since it belongs to a different company and you did not need it removed.
The address bar route for a site you have open

If the site is already open, you can skip the search. The website settings icon sits to the left of the address bar. This route comes from iDownloadBlog's 2025 guide, not from Google's help page, so check the labels in your window before you click.

items: Open the site, then click the website settings icon to the left of the address bar.
Click the trash icon next to that site's entry to delete its data.

blocks.text: This route is quick when the site is already open. If the site is not open, use the Settings route above.
Open the full list with chrome://settings/content/all

Some third-party guides suggest typing chrome://settings/content/all into the address bar. That address opens the site list directly, so you skip the menu clicks. I found this only in those guides, not on Google's help page, so treat it as a convenience rather than a guarantee.
Once the list opens, the search box and trash icon work the same way as in Settings. If the address does nothing, go back to the Settings route. Trying it does no harm.
Why Command+Shift+Delete is the wrong tool here

Command+Shift+Delete is the one Mac shortcut I found for clearing data. It opens the Clear browsing data dialog for all sites, not one. A 2023 How-To Geek article describes the dialog. It offers time ranges such as last hour, last 24 hours, last week, and all time.

It also lists data types, including cookies and cached files. Use that dialog when many sites misbehave at once. For one site, it overreaches, because clearing all browser data signs you out of every site you are logged into, according to iDownloadBlog.
Check that the data is gone

Reload the site in a new tab. Then return to the site list and search for its domain again. The row should be gone. If you are still signed in, look for the site's own sign-out button, because it may keep your session on its servers.
Expect the site to store data again as soon as you visit it. Clearing is a reset, not a block. If the same problem returns, the cause may lie with the site rather than with what was stored.
Common mistakes people make

items: Searching for the full web address instead of the domain, so the row never shows up.
Clicking the trash icon on the wrong row. Read the domain before you click.
Using Command+Shift+Delete when only one site is the problem, which signs you out everywhere.
Expecting clearing to stop tracking. Consumer Reports quotes a privacy director saying companies can track with non-cookie technologies.
Forgetting that the site stores fresh data the next time you visit it.

blocks.text: Who clears site data, and how often

All About Cookies surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults in September 2023 and again in August 2025. About 80% said they know how to clear or disable cookies. That figure is self-reported, so it shows confidence, not skill.

The same survey found that 24% blindly accept all cookies when prompted. A Statista chart reports that about one in ten U.S. adults usually refuse cookies. That chart does not state its survey year or sample size, so treat it as a rough signal.
When one-site clearing is the wrong fix

Clear one site when only that site misbehaves. If several sites break together, the cause may be your network, a browser extension, or Chrome itself. Clearing one site's data is unlikely to fix those.
It also will not stop tracking. Use the cookie controls for ongoing protection. The [cookie blocking guide](/how-to/block-third-party-cookies-in-chrome) walks through those settings.
Next steps after you clear a site

If the problem returns, check the site's support notes or status page first. A broken site is not always a local problem. If the site keeps setting cookies you do not want, block them for future visits.

For the wider cleanup, read [how to clear browsing data in Chrome](/how-to/clear-browsing-data-in-chrome). If you want to test a site in a clean window, check the [incognito window guide](/how-to/open-an-incognito-window-in-chrome) for how that window handles your data.

faq.question: Will clearing one site's data sign me out of everything?
faq.answer: No. Clearing one site's data affects that site only. You may be signed out of that site, but your other sites keep their sign-ins. The all-sites option behaves differently. iDownloadBlog says it signs you out of every site you are logged into.

faq.question: Do I need to restart Chrome after clearing site data?
faq.answer: You can test without restarting. Reload the site in a new tab and check the result. If the problem stays, search the site list again to confirm the row is gone.

faq.question: Why can't I find the trash icon or the Remove label?
faq.answer: Your search may be too specific, or the site may store data under a different domain. Try a shorter search term. If your Mac is managed by a work or school account, an admin policy may block changes, so ask your IT team.

faq.question: Does deleting site data sign me out of my Google Account?
faq.answer: Google says deleting cookies while you are signed in to Chrome does not sign you out of your Google Account. That statement is on Google's Android help page, so check your own sign-in after you clear.

faq.question: Is there a Mac shortcut that clears data for one website?
faq.answer: I did not find one. Command+Shift+Delete opens Clear browsing data for all sites. For one site, use the Settings route or the address bar route in this guide.

faq.question: Does clearing site data stop tracking?
faq.answer: Not completely. Consumer Reports quotes its privacy director saying companies may use non-cookie technologies to track you, and clearing cookies does not address that.

faq.question: Why does the site remember me again so quickly?
faq.answer: Visiting the site again lets it set new cookies and data. Clearing resets the site, but it does not stop the site from storing data again. Blocking third-party cookies limits some of that storage.

task: Clear site data for one website in Chrome on Mac
appliesTo: Google Chrome desktop on macOS, current versions
requirements: A Mac with Google Chrome installed and open
The website's domain, such as example.com
Your sign-in details for that site, or a way to reset your password

steps.name: Open Chrome Settings
steps.text: Click the three-dot More icon at the top right of Chrome, then choose Settings.
steps.tip: The three-dot icon sits at the right end of Chrome's toolbar.

steps.name: Open Privacy and security
steps.text: Click Privacy and security, then click Third-party cookies.
steps.tip: If you cannot find an item, use the search box at the top of Settings.

steps.name: Open See all site data and permissions
steps.text: Click See all site data and permissions. Chrome shows every site that has stored data on your Mac.
menuPath: See all site data and permissions
steps.tip: This list can be long. Use the search box to shrink it.

steps.name: Search for the site
steps.text: Type the domain into the search box, such as example.com. Leave out https:// and any path after the domain.
steps.tip: If nothing shows, try a shorter part of the name, such as example.

steps.name: Click the trash icon labeled Remove
steps.text: Find the row for the site. Click the trash icon labeled Remove at the right end of that row.
steps.tip: Read the domain on the row before you click. Two sites can have similar names.

steps.name: Confirm with Delete
steps.text: A confirmation appears. Click Delete to remove that site's cookies and stored data.
steps.tip: The deletion applies only to the site you chose, not to every site in the list.

steps.name: Check the result
steps.text: Search for the domain again. If the row is gone, reload the site in a new tab to confirm the change.
steps.tip: The site may store data again the next time you visit it.

shortcuts.action: Open Clear browsing data (all sites, not one site)

troubleshooting.problem: The Remove trash icon is missing
troubleshooting.fix: Search again with a shorter term, since the row may be stored under a different domain. If a work or school account manages the Mac, an admin policy may block changes, so ask IT.

troubleshooting.problem: I am still signed in after clearing
troubleshooting.fix: Some sites keep your session on their own servers, so clearing on your Mac does not end it. Use the site's sign-out button, then sign in again.

troubleshooting.problem: The site still shows old content
troubleshooting.fix: Close the tab, open the site in a new tab, and check again. If the old content stays, search the site list for other rows that share the domain and clear those too.

troubleshooting.problem: The data came back the next day
troubleshooting.fix: Visiting the site creates data again. Clearing resets it. If the site keeps setting data you do not want, block third-party cookies or accept that the site will store data again.

troubleshooting.problem: Clearing did not fix the problem
troubleshooting.fix: The cause may be the site, an extension, or Chrome itself. Test the site in another browser to find out which one is at fault.
